I am a 50-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been working this land since I was a teenager. My family has about 7 mu of flat, good-quality land here on the North China Plain. I only finished primary school, but I know my fields well — better than any book.

The wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October, as I always do. This spring, I will topdress it with urea when it greens up and jointing starts, and I will irrigate three times: once now to help it recover from winter, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I also need to spray for weeds, aphids, and the fungal diseases that always come when the weather turns humid. I use an improved wheat variety that my neighbor saved seed from — it performs reliably here. Before sowing last autumn, I rotary-tilled the field and put down compound fertilizer as a basal dressing.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. I never waste time between crops — the season is short. I buy hybrid maize seed every year; the hybrids yield much more than keeping my own seed, and the seed dealer here sells good ones. I will use no-tillage direct seeding right after the wheat comes off — that saves me time, fuel, and keeps moisture in the soil. I will spread compound fertilizer at sowing, irrigate twice (once after sowing if it is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage), and spray for weeds and armyworms. 

I do not grow vegetables or cotton. Those crops are risky — the prices jump around, and if I guess wrong, I lose money. Wheat and maize have stable purchase prices, and the grain station buys them every year. I am too old to take big risks with my family's food security.
